issues.issue: 'the amounts reasonably required for the purposes of the Fund' governs when MTC may divert excess money, without any mechanism for determining that amount.
Section 4.6.1 makes the Fund the source of the Operator's mandatory upgrade obligations, yet this Section allows MTC to spend excess Fund money on other network purposes.

The decommissioning contribution is payable 'within thirty (30) days after the end of each calendar year' but is described as funding decommissioning 'at such other time as MTC determines', with MTC free in its 'sole discretion' to spend the money on anything within MBI's mission.

Payments start 'on the Effective Date' whereas Section 4.9.8 provides that payments to MTC are quarterly unless otherwise specified, and Section 4.9.6 keys the parallel CAPEX contribution to the Commencement Date.
The quarterly default is displaced by annual payment dates in Sections 4.9.5 and 4.9.7, so the provision only operates residually and its field of application is unclear.
'assets, liabilities, income expenses' omits a conjunction, and 'sufficient information and analysis' to MTC's 'reasonable satisfaction' sets no defined deliverable.
'no fraud or intentional or willful misconduct by any Person' certifies as to persons outside the Operator's knowledge, and 'Person' is capitalised but undefined.

The restriction combines a duration test ('more than two (2) years') with an IFRS revenue-recognition test in a single sentence, so it is unclear whether both conditions must be met or either suffices.

The maintenance standard is set by specifications 'contained or incorporated, or to be contained or incorporated, in MTC's agreement with its Design-Build Contractor' and by 'the standards for carrier class networks', neither of which is fixed in this instrument.
The Operator is bound to specifications in a contract to which it is not a party, while Section 12.1 makes this Agreement the entire agreement on the Services.

'appropriate Scheduled Maintenance' measured by the Operator's own 'then current preventative maintenance procedures, which shall meet or exceed standard industry practice' allows the obligor to set its own standard.
'MTC may not prevent Network Operator from performing maintenance that Network Operator deems necessary' is absolute, and the following sentence calls MTC's right to be present 'this requirement'.

The unqualified statement that MTC may not prevent maintenance sits against Section 4.1's reservation of 'reasonable oversight by MTC' and Section 4.11.7's requirement of an MTC-approved procedures manual.
'any potential service-affecting situation' and 'any event imminently likely to cause' failure set no ascertainable trigger for the emergency and non-emergency categories.
'credible notification by any third party' is an undefined standard for triggering dispatch.
'workmanlike care' and 'reasonably cooperate ... in analyzing the disturbances' are open-textured standards with no benchmark.
Section 5.1.8 promises performance 'in accordance with or exceeding generally accepted industry standards', a different and higher standard than 'workmanlike care' here.
The manual must 'ensure that SLAs are met' although Section 4.13.1 records that the SLA was still being completed when the Agreement was signed.
'such information and documentation ... that may be required' identifies the obligation only by reference to unspecified future insurance and recovery needs.
'a claim or series of claims arising out of a single event totaling more than $500,000' does not say whether the threshold is measured by claimed amount, settled amount or proceeds.
Proceeds must be applied to repair or replacement here, while Section 4.11.8.2 and Section 2.45 divert rental-loss proceeds into Network Revenue subject to revenue sharing.
'net of legal fees or other extraordinary costs of recovery outside of normal claim adjustment costs' draws a line between normal and extraordinary costs that is nowhere defined.
Section 2.45 states that Network Revenue 'shall include the proceeds of any rental loss insurance coverage', without the net-of-costs qualification this Section adds.
'as quickly as possible (allowing for delays caused by circumstances beyond the reasonable control of Network Operator)' sets a response standard with no measurable content.
This open-ended standard sits against the specific service levels the SLA is to contain under Section 4.13.1 and the KPI regime of Section 4.13.3.
Free subcontracting of maintenance sits against Section 12.10's prohibition on assigning the Agreement in whole or in part without consent.
'Segments of the MTC Network' is capitalised as if referring to the defined 'Network Segment', and the Section does not say who bears the cost of the testing MTC directs.
'full compliance with all Network Policies' is absolute, but Section 2.44 lets MTC add policies unilaterally and Section 4.7.4.1 lets MTC exempt dark fiber leases from them.
The performance standard is fixed by 'the SLA the Parties are in the process of completing', a document that did not exist at signing, so the operative standard was left to future agreement.
The cross-reference to Sections 4.9.2.4 and 4.9.2.5 is astray: those provisions govern MTC's agreements with third parties and an incremental-cost credit, not the completion of the SLA.
'will review and agree to commercially reasonable changes' is an agreement to agree, resolved only by a further duty to 'deal with each other in good faith'.
The Section gives no route to resolution if the Parties do not agree, which sits against Section 6.2's requirement of express written approval of both Parties for any change.
Performance is measured against KPIs 'as the same may evolve and be supplemented and enhanced during the Term', without saying who may change them.
Section 6.1.1(ii) gives the IPT only a recommending role over KPIs, and Section 6.2 requires both Parties' written approval, so unilateral evolution of KPIs is not supported.

Records must be kept 'at least seven (7) years after the end of the Term' here, while Section 4.1.3 requires seven years 'beyond the Term' and Section 3.6.1.2 requires seven years for discount documentation, creating overlapping regimes.
'Network Operator shall promptly make all remunerative payments to MTC' uses 'remunerative' in an unnatural sense and provides no reciprocal adjustment where the error favours MTC.
A twenty-four hour notice requirement here sits against Section 4.14.1's grant of access 'at all reasonable times' without notice.
'any changes and take other actions which are necessary in order to maintain compliance' is unbounded and does not address who bears the cost.
'unless expressly constructed otherwise' is a mechanical error for 'construed', and the sentence turns on which reading is taken.
The denial of any leasehold or similar interest sits against Section 3.6.1, which grants the Operator a right to lease dark fiber through an IRU on the same network.
'necessary or appropriate' resources 'however described' is an open-ended cost allocation with no boundary.
The general duty to pay for all resources sits against Section 4.6.1's CAPEX Fund mechanism and Section 4.9.1's carve-outs for construction and MBI Extension costs.
'an adequate number of trained and qualified personnel as necessary or appropriate' fixes no measurable staffing obligation.
'reasonable access' 'as necessary or appropriate' does not say whether MTC may condition or refuse access the Operator considers essential.
'an office ... which shall be the headquarters for the Network Operator' does not say whether the corporate headquarters must relocate to Massachusetts or only a project office be maintained.
Section 12.12.2 gives the Operator's notice address in Calgary, Alberta, which sits awkwardly with a covenant that its headquarters be in Massachusetts.
'in line with industry best practices' and 'no less stringent than the then-current requirements of MassDOT, ITD and EOPSS' import moving external standards with no fixed content.
The duty to 'deny such access to all other persons' sits against Section 4.14.1, which requires access for MTC's auditors, inspectors, regulators and other designated representatives.
'a legal, valid and binding obligation of such Party' uses 'such Party' with no antecedent in a representation made only by the Network Operator.
Section 12.14 makes the Agreement binding 'only upon condition that' the parent delivers a guaranty, which sits against an unqualified representation that the Agreement is already binding.

The representation covers the parent company and 'any of their respective officers, directors or Affiliates', a class the Operator cannot fully know, and 'threatened' criminal investigations have no defined test.
The representation is stated to continue 'throughout the Term', which cannot literally be true of a warranty as to conduct 'at all times since January 1, 2005'.
'services that are substantially equivalent to the Services in other settings and circumstances' is a warranty of past experience with no measurable content.
'in accordance with or exceeding generally accepted industry standards' is an undefined benchmark.
This general industry standard sits against Section 4.13.1's promise to meet the (then unwritten) SLA standards and Section 4.11.6's lower 'workmanlike care'.
The representation is stated to continue throughout the Term although it is framed as to matters 'not disclosed to MTC or its designee prior to the Effective Date'.
'timely and diligently cooperate to effect the goals, objectives and purposes of this Agreement' is an open-ended covenant with no measurable content.
'self-dealing' is undefined and the covenant to protect 'the interests of MTC as owner' in all third-party transactions has no stated boundary.

Section 4.8 expressly permits an Affiliate of the Operator to contract with it as a Third Party Service Provider, and Sections 2.43 and 4.5.5 contemplate the Operator trading with itself on its own Extensions.
The Operator covenants to comply with Article 5 of a Master Services Agreement that was 'currently being negotiated' and therefore had unknown content at signing.

The cross-reference to 'Sections 4.9.2.4 and 4.9.2.5' is astray, as those provisions deal with MTC's negotiation of third-party agreements and an incremental-cost credit, not the finalisation of this covenant.

The representation that all required insurance 'has been taken out' as of the Effective Date sits against Section 10.3.3, which allows thirty days after the Effective Date for certificates and later procurement of some coverages.

'ensure that the MTC Network is and remains, in compliance with all Network Policies, laws, regulations, and orders' is an absolute guarantee of a state of affairs partly outside the Operator's control.
'immediately in writing' sets no ascertainable deadline.
'such Party' has no antecedent within this MTC representation.
Section 12.14 conditions the Agreement's becoming binding on delivery of a parent guaranty, which sits against an unqualified representation that it is already binding.
'timely and diligently cooperate to effect the goals, objectives and purposes of this Agreement' has no measurable content.

Purpose (iv) gives the IPT power 'to resolve disputes submitted by the Parties pursuant to ARTICLE 11', while Section 11.1.1.3 gives it only a duty to discuss and negotiate before escalation and arbitration.

The IPT includes a representative of EOPSS and ITD who are not Parties, yet Section 11.1.3 allows the IPT to stay arbitration time periods 'upon unanimous vote of its members', giving a non-party a veto over the Parties' dispute process.
An IPT that need meet only once a year sits against Section 11.1.1.2, which requires it to 'meet as often as necessary' in a dispute, and against the fifteen-day resolution window in Section 11.1.2.
Limb (ii) says the Parties 'may either negotiate to amend the Agreement ... or consider the change during any subsequent renewal', so no change is ever compelled.
Section 4.7.5 makes the Price Caps amendable 'pursuant to ARTICLE 6', but this Section supplies no mechanism that can produce an amendment without both Parties' agreement.
'promptly deliver to the requesting party any and all Confidential Information' on request 'at any time' is unqualified and would require return of information needed for continued performance.

Each Party being 'the exclusive owner' of its own Confidential Information cannot be squared with Section 7.3.4, which declares all written and electronic materials containing Confidential Information 'the sole and exclusive property of MTC'.

MTC's public-records disclosure obligations sit against Section 2.9's inclusion of 'the existence, terms and conditions of this Agreement' in Confidential Information and against Section 7.3.1's absolute non-disclosure duty.
The Operator must comply with confidentiality policies 'as communicated by MTC's Executive Director or General Counsel ... from time to time', which allows unilateral variation of its obligations.
Unilateral communication of new policy obligations conflicts with Section 12.1, which permits amendment only by written document signed by both Parties.
The exceptions are limited to fulfilment of obligations and General Counsel direction, while Section 7.5 supplies a wider set of exceptions to the same Section 7.3 duties.
'any Person related to or that is an Affiliate of with Network Operator' is ungrammatical, and 'any Applicable Third Party' is capitalised but never defined.
Article 2 provides that all capitalised terms take their meanings from that Article, yet 'Applicable Third Party' appears nowhere in it.
'To the maximum extent required by law, Network Operator shall indemnify' is an odd formulation ('required' rather than 'permitted'), and 'MTC's Written Materials' is capitalised but undefined.
Making all such materials 'the sole and exclusive property of MTC' cannot be squared with Section 7.1, under which each Party exclusively owns the Confidential Information it furnishes.
The exceptions are conditioned on proof 'through written records' and use the undefined capitalised terms 'Governmental Authority' and 'Applicable Third Party'.
The carve-outs are expressed to apply only to 'obligations under Section 7.3', leaving the parallel obligations in Sections 7.1 and 7.2 unqualified.

'a series of non-material or persistent breaches ... that, in the aggregate, have a material and significant adverse impact' has no measurable threshold, and the change-of-control test — control 'through the ownership of at least fifty percent (50%) of the voting securities' — is ambiguous as to whether ownership is required at all.

Termination for cause here drives Section 3.6.1 and 3.6.2, which strip the Operator's dark fiber rights, and Section 8.4.1, which says the Term is not deemed terminated until transfer assistance is complete.

The charge 'increas[es] the percentage of Network Revenue owed ... under Section 4.9.5' by half a point, but Section 4.9.5 contains three different percentages (0%, 4% and 20%), so which percentage is increased is not stated.
The charge is available for any Section 8.1 ground except 8.1.4, yet Sections 8.1.2 and 8.1.3 provide no notice-and-cure period from which the 'initial thirty (30) days' can be measured.
'a disruption to the basic functioning of more than fifty percent (50%) of the MTC Network' gives no measure — by mileage, strands, customers or revenue — for the fifty percent threshold.
'as soon as is reasonably practicable by one acting with urgency' compounds two open standards to fix the extension of time.

This excuse for Force Majeure failures sits against Section 12.2, which excuses nonperformance only where caused by the other Party's default, and against Section 11.2's duty of continued performance.
